concept.name: Three white soldiers
concept.definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long white candles with progressively higher closes, each closing at or near its high and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained buying marking a bottom after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
concept.intuition: Three sessions in a row of determined buying, each marching higher and finishing near its highs, suggests the market has been taken over by confident bulls rather than one-day short covering.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: three long white bodies with C1 < C2 < C3; each candle opens within the previous body (no big gaps) and closes near its high (small upper shadows). Appearing after a downtrend or at support, the pattern's steady structure is meant to distinguish genuine accumulation from a spike.
concept.failure_modes: After three strong up candles the market is often short-term overbought, so the pattern frequently completes right before a pullback; late entry is a common way it 'fails'. Very large first or third candles can also signal exhaustion rather than sustained demand.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a signal to chase price higher indefinitely; many practitioners use it to time entries on the ensuing retracement rather than buying the third candle's close. Gapped, non-overlapping opens do not form the classic pattern.
concept.example: After a slide to 45.00, a stock prints three consecutive daily candles closing at 46.20, 47.40, and 48.60, each opening inside the prior body and closing near its high. Chartists read the three white soldiers as evidence of a durable bottom.
